explanations.explanation: You've got Daniel's words right. He says, “…and the longer one grew up later.” So the tall one showed up after the short one and still ended up taller. Late to the shift and finished with the biggest batch, friend.
I get why you'd pick it. Whoever grows first usually wins the height contest. But Daniel says the longer one grew up later. That's the one that got the late start.

Daniel doesn't describe the horns growing in together. He says one was longer than the other, and the longer one grew up later. So there's a timing gap in the picture. Same oven, different bake times.
Daniel says the opposite. No animal could stand against the ram, and there was no deliverance from his power. Nobody was holding a line against him. That ram had the whole road to himself.

Right, because Daniel says no animal could stand against him. There was also no deliverance from his power. Nobody got in his way and nobody rescued anyone. He did as he pleased, and that's the whole picture.
That's the word. Daniel says the ram “did as he pleased and became great.” Three directions, nobody standing against him, and the verse lands on great. I'd have settled for a clean countertop.

Weary is a fair guess, since a lot of charging is going on. But the verse never says the ram is tired. It says he did as he pleased and became great. Weary is more my speed, usually around the fifth beep of the oven timer.

Nothing in the verse says the ram is afraid. He's the one doing the charging, and no animal could stand against him. Daniel says he did as he pleased and became great. The fear in this verse isn't on the ram's side.
Yes, a horn. Daniel sees a goat “with a prominent horn between his eyes.” One big horn right in the middle, which makes this goat easy to pick out of a crowd.
A crown is a natural guess for something that stands out on a head. But Daniel doesn't see a crown. He sees a goat with a prominent horn between his eyes. Same spot on the head, different item.
No sparkle in this verse, friend. Daniel says the goat has a prominent horn between his eyes. No jewels, no bling, just one horn right in the middle.

explanations.answer: He rushes at him with furious power
explanations.explanation: That's how Daniel puts it: the goat “rushed at him with furious power.” Verse 7 adds that he approached the ram in a rage. No warm-up lap, no polite hello. Just full speed from the start.

explanations.answer: He walks up to him slowly and calmly
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what Daniel sees. The goat rushes at the ram with furious power, and verse 7 says he's in a rage against him. Nobody's strolling in this scene. This goat skipped the walk entirely.

explanations.answer: He stops short and stares him down
explanations.explanation: There's no staring contest in this vision. Daniel says the goat rushed at the ram with furious power. Then verse 7 says he struck the ram. This goat doesn't stop to think about it.

explanations.answer: The goat throws him down and tramples him
explanations.explanation: That's what Daniel sees. The goat “threw him to the ground and trampled him.” The ram was powerless to stand against him. The same ram that did as he pleased now can't get up.

explanations.answer: He escapes across the Ulai Canal
explanations.explanation: Daniel never sees the ram getting away. He says the ram was powerless to stand against the goat. Then the goat threw him to the ground and trampled him. The canal doesn't come into it.

explanations.answer: Another ram comes to rescue him
explanations.explanation: No second ram shows up in Daniel's vision. He says no one could deliver the ram from the goat's power. The goat threw him to the ground and trampled him. When the text says no one, it means no one.

Yes. Daniel says that when the large horn broke off, four prominent horns came up in its place. They pointed toward the four winds of heaven. One horn goes out and four come in. That's quite the replacement policy.
The large horn doesn't leave an empty spot. Daniel says four prominent horns came up in its place. They pointed toward the four winds of heaven. So something does come up where the big horn was.

The word little is misleading here. Daniel says the horn “grew extensively” toward the south, the east and the Beautiful Land. Verse 10 says it grew as high as the host of heaven. So it doesn't stay small at all.

Correct. This horn starts little and doesn't stay that way. Daniel says it grew extensively toward the south, the east and the Beautiful Land. Then verse 10 says it grew as high as the host of heaven. Little is just where it starts.
That's right. Daniel says the horn “cast down some of the host and some of the stars to the earth and trampled them.” Notice it says some, not all. It's a heavy moment, so I'll just say it plainly.

Daniel says it does happen. The horn cast down some of the host and some of the stars to the earth and trampled them. It says some of them, which is exactly what the text gives. I think this is one of the heavier lines in the vision.

explanations.answer: It prospers in whatever it does
explanations.explanation: That's what Daniel says. The horn “flung truth to the ground and prospered in whatever it did.” The host and the daily sacrifice were given over to it. This is a heavy part of the vision, and Daniel doesn't soften it.

explanations.answer: It shrinks back down to little
explanations.explanation: Nothing in this verse shrinks. Daniel says the horn flung truth to the ground and prospered in whatever it did. It started little and grew. At this point in the vision it's still on the way up.

explanations.answer: It turns on the other horns
explanations.explanation: Daniel never says that. He says the host and the daily sacrifice were given over to the horn. He says it flung truth to the ground and prospered in whatever it did. The text doesn't mention the other horns here.

explanations.answer: How long until it is fulfilled
explanations.explanation: That's the question. One holy one asks, “How long until the fulfillment of the vision…” It's about the daily sacrifice, the rebellion and the trampled sanctuary. Everybody asks how long when they've been standing in a slow line at the bank.

The question isn't about who. The holy one asks how long until the fulfillment of the vision. That covers the daily sacrifice, the rebellion and the trampled sanctuary. He's asking about time, not names.

The sanctuary comes up in the question, but not where it stands. The holy one asks how long until the fulfillment of the vision. That includes the surrender of the sanctuary and the host to be trampled. The question is about how long.
Yes. The answer is, “It will take 2,300 evenings and mornings; then the sanctuary will be properly restored.” The trampling has an end. After the count, the sanctuary is restored.

The text says the opposite. After the 2,300 evenings and mornings, “the sanctuary will be properly restored.” So the answer ends with restoration, like a counter wiped clean after the flour cloud finally settles.
That's the one. The voice says, “Gabriel, explain the vision to this man.” Gabriel is an angel who stands in the presence of God (Luke 1:19). Daniel needed someone to explain this one.

Michael is a name you'll meet elsewhere in Daniel, where he's called one of the chief princes (Daniel 10:13). But the voice here doesn't call for him. It says, “Gabriel, explain the vision to this man.”

Nathan was a prophet who spoke to King David (2 Samuel 12:1), but he isn't in this scene. The voice by the Ulai calls for Gabriel to explain the vision to Daniel. Different name, different story, friend.
That's what Gabriel says. He tells Daniel, “…understand that the vision concerns the time of the end.” So this isn't a small vision about one afternoon. Gabriel points it toward the end.
Gabriel doesn't say that here. He tells Daniel, “…understand that the vision concerns the time of the end.” Babylon isn't named in his words. So his answer points to the time of the end.
Gabriel doesn't say the vision is about Daniel's own future. He says the vision concerns the time of the end. That's bigger than one man's calendar, and I'd say Daniel's to-do list was safe.
Gabriel doesn't leave Daniel on the floor. Daniel says Gabriel touched him and helped him to his feet. So the deep sleep with his face to the ground isn't where it ends.
Right. Daniel says Gabriel “touched me, helped me to my feet.” So Daniel doesn't stay face down. Gabriel picks him up and then keeps talking.
That's it. Gabriel says, “the large horn between his eyes is the first king.” So the big horn stands for a person, and the goat stands for the king of Greece.
Gabriel doesn't say city. He says the large horn between the shaggy goat's eyes is the first king. The goat stands for the king of Greece. So the horn is a king.
Gabriel doesn't call the horn an army. He says the large horn between the goat's eyes is the first king. It's one person at the front.

Yes. Gabriel says these are four kingdoms that will rise from that nation, “…but will not have the same power.” So they're four and none of them matches the first. That's the horn that broke, replaced by lesser ones.
Gabriel says the opposite. The four kingdoms will rise from that nation but “will not have the same power.” So they don't match the first horn's strength.
Gabriel says his power will be great, but it will not be his own. So the first half fits and the second half doesn't. I won't guess whose power it is, because the verse doesn't say.
That's right. Gabriel says, “His power will be great, but it will not be his own.” Great power, borrowed. Think of someone using another person's oven and calling the whole batch theirs.
Yes, deceit. Gabriel says, “Through his craft and by his hand, he will cause deceit to prosper…” This king is skilled in intrigue, and his deceit does well. It's a heavy thing to hear.
Gabriel doesn't say justice. He says that through his craft and by his hand, the king will cause deceit to prosper. Justice would be a very different kind of verse.
Kindness doesn't show up in this verse, friend. Gabriel says the king will cause deceit to prosper through his craft and by his hand. Nothing gentle about this king.

explanations.answer: He will be broken off but not by human hands
explanations.explanation: That's what Gabriel says. “Yet he will be broken off, but not by human hands.” He stands against the Prince of princes, and he's still broken off. The verse says no more than that, so I won't add anything.

explanations.answer: He will be defeated by a great human army
explanations.explanation: Gabriel says it's not by human hands. He says the king “will be broken off, but not by human hands.” So no human army is named as the one who does it.

explanations.answer: He will keep ruling until his old age
explanations.explanation: Gabriel says the king will be broken off. It's not a quiet retirement. He says, “Yet he will be broken off, but not by human hands.”

explanations.answer: Because it concerns the distant future
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Gabriel gives. He says, “Now you must seal up the vision, for it concerns the distant future.” Gabriel says the vision is true, then tells Daniel to seal it. The reason is in the same verse.

explanations.answer: Because it is too frightening to share
explanations.explanation: Gabriel doesn't give that reason. He says, “Now you must seal up the vision, for it concerns the distant future.” So the reason he gives is about time.

explanations.answer: Because the king would not believe it
explanations.explanation: The verse says nothing about the king believing it or not. Gabriel says to seal up the vision because it concerns the distant future. The reason he gives is the future.

explanations.answer: He goes about the king's business
explanations.explanation: That's what Daniel says. “Then I got up and went about the king's business.” Sick days end and the work doesn't. He goes back to it after the vision and the days in bed.
Daniel doesn't go to Jerusalem in this passage. He says he got up and went about the king's business. So he heads back to work, not on a trip.

explanations.answer: He tells the whole city everything
explanations.explanation: Daniel doesn't say he tells anyone anything here. He says he got up and went about the king's business. Gabriel had told him to seal up the vision (Daniel 8:26).

Daniel says otherwise. He writes, “I was confounded by the vision; it was beyond understanding.” So he's still puzzled, even after Gabriel's explanation. If the man who saw the vision says it's beyond understanding, I'm in good company.
Right. Daniel says, “I was confounded by the vision; it was beyond understanding.” So he doesn't walk away with all of it figured out. He saw it and Gabriel explained it, and he still says that.
